passage: Friday night. I asked Papa straight out today: "What are you actually afraid of?" He looked tired and said, "I don't want you to be alone when we're old. And I don't want to be alone either, if something happens to your mother or me. Health is not something we can plan." I had not expected that. All this time I thought it was about relatives and status. I have never heard him use the word "afraid" before. So tonight I changed my plan. It now includes a visit home every month, a shared calendar for hospital check-ups so I know about them, and two holidays a year with them. Marriage is still later. But now the plan answers his real fear. Vandana

qa.q: What did Papa say he was afraid of?
qa.a: Papa said he did not want Vandana to be alone when they are old, and worried about health not being something to plan.

qa.q: How did Vandana feel on hearing what Papa feared?
qa.a: Vandana was surprised, because Vandana had believed the trouble was about relatives and status.

qa.q: What else could Vandana add to the plan, and why?
qa.a: Vandana could offer to help Papa keep a list of family contacts and doctors, since it shows care for the fear he named.

qa.q: How might Papa see the new plan with regular visits?
qa.a: Papa is likely to feel comforted and heard, since the plan speaks to his worry about health and being alone.

grounding: After hearing that a parent's real fear is health and loneliness in old age, a young adult adds visits and shared responsibilities to the plan.

subtopic: Talking with parents about marriage pressure
subtype: Approach: adjusting the plan after hearing a parent's constraint [Revision]
passage:
In their small house in the old part of Hubballi, Vasudha's mother had raised marriage at every meal since Vasudha got the job offer in Pune. That evening, while Eshaan, her younger brother, cleared the plates, Vasudha finally asked, 'Amma, what are you really worried about?'
Her mother was quiet. Then: 'Since your father went, the nights are long. My knees are bad. Eshaan will leave too. If you're married, at least someone will be looking after you, and maybe after me.'
Vasudha felt her throat tighten. It had never been about the wedding.
'Amma, I'm still taking the job. But listen.' She thought aloud. 'I'll come home every second weekend. I'll set up video calls so you can see me every night. And Eshaan and I will split your hospital visits: he takes the ones in term time, I take the holidays.'
Eshaan nodded from the sink. 'Deal.'
Her mother wiped her eyes and, for once, didn't mention marriage.

qa.q: How often will Vasudha come home?
How did Vasudha feel when her mother explained, and why?
qa.a: Her throat tightened with sadness and sympathy as she saw that the pressure came from loneliness and fear, not the wedding.

qa.q: What else could Vasudha do in Pune to reassure her mother?
qa.a: Keep to the nightly video calls and tell her mother the plan can change if her health needs more help.

qa.q: How might Eshaan feel about splitting the hospital visits?
qa.a: Eshaan seems ready and willing, glad to share the care of their mother.

grounding: Shows a young adult learning a parent's real fear is health and being alone, and adding regular visits and shared care to the plan.
